name: X
tagline: Global public microblogging feed with paid tiers for longer posts, edits, a checkmark and revenue share.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. X has changed tier names and prices repeatedly.

verdictSummary: You can absolutely build a microblog in an afternoon: posts, replies, likes, a reverse-chronological feed, media uploads. What you cannot build is the several hundred million other people who show up to read it. Every feature X charges for is a cosmetic layer on top of an audience you do not have: longer posts nobody reads, edits to posts nobody saw, a checkmark next to a name nobody recognizes. The paid tier is not software, it is preferential placement inside someone else's crowd. The closest honest DIY is a private archive plus a feed reader, which is a different product with a different point.
coreLoopDIY: A self-hosted single-user microblog that publishes short posts to your own domain with an RSS feed, plus a local reader that pulls in the handful of accounts and sites you actually follow.
requirements: A domain and somewhere to host a small Node process
RSS or Atom feeds for whatever you want to follow, since scraping X is against terms and the API is priced for companies
Your X data export if you want the archive half
whatYouLose: The audience, which is the entire product
Reach mechanics: algorithmic amplification, quote posts, trending, the chance a stranger sees you
Anyone to reply to you, and any reason for them to
Verification and creator payouts, both of which only exist because the network exists
Mobile apps, push notifications, DMs with people who are not you
moatNotes: Network effects here are unusually asymmetric: the value is not that your friends are on it, it is that strangers, journalists and people you are arguing with are on it. That cannot be forked.
whyPeopleStillPay: Almost nobody pays X for features. They pay for placement: replies ranked higher, longer posts allowed, a badge that signals you are not a throwaway account, and in some cases a payout tied to impressions you can only earn inside the network. It is closer to buying advertising than buying software. That is exactly why a self-hosted clone is a category error rather than a cheaper option.
notes: The software is a weekend project; the crowd is not. The moat is a few hundred million people already standing in one room, and the paid tier just sells you a better spot in it.
prompt:
Build a self-hosted personal microblog and feed reader. Single user, runs on my own domain. This is not an X clone: there are no other users, no follows, no DMs, no algorithm.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Node 20 with TypeScript
- Hono for the HTTP server
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, single file at ./data/app.db
- Server-rendered HTML with plain templates and one hand-written CSS file, no React, no Tailwind
- Vitest for a handful of tests

What to build:
1. Post composer at /admin behind a single password from ADMIN_PASSWORD in .env, session cookie signed with SESSION_SECRET. No user accounts table, no OAuth.
2. Posts: body text up to 5000 chars, optional image uploads stored on disk in ./data/uploads, created_at, optional reply_to for self-threading.
3. Public timeline at / in reverse chronological order, permalinks at /p/:id, thread view that shows a post plus its self-replies.
4. RSS and Atom feeds at /feed.xml and /atom.xml over my posts.
5. Feed reader: a follows table of RSS/Atom URLs, a fetch job that polls them on an interval and stores entries, a reading view at /reading with unread counts and mark-as-read. Use a well-maintained feed parser. Do not scrape any social network and do not touch the X API.
6. Import: a CLI script that ingests an X data export tweets.js file into an /archive section, full text search over it with SQLite FTS5. Archive posts are clearly marked as imported and excluded from the public feeds unless a flag is set.

Explicitly out of scope: likes, follower counts, notifications, ActivityPub, mobile apps, analytics, telemetry, any third-party service.

Deliver a README with setup, a .env.example, a single npm run dev command, and a Dockerfile. Keep the whole thing under roughly 1500 lines and readable.
